text: Fuzz tests still call one function, once, per run. Real contracts get broken by sequences: deposit, deposit, withdraw, deposit, withdraw, withdraw — hundreds of calls in random order, from random actors. An invariant is a property that has to stay true no matter what that sequence looks like — for example, this vault can never pay out more ETH than was ever deposited into it.

targetContract() tells Forge which contract to fuzz calls against. Forge then generates a random sequence of calls to that contract's public functions, checking an invariant_SolvencyCheck function after every single call in the sequence, not just once at the end.

Fuzzing a contract's raw public functions directly usually wastes most of the run on calls Forge can't constrain. Real suites wrap the contract in a handler that constrains inputs the same way bound() did, and tracks cumulative state as ghost variables — off-chain tracking that doesn't exist on the real contract, kept purely so the invariant can check the real balance against what the handler actually sent.

targetContract() then points at the handler, not the vault directly, so Forge only calls the constrained, trackable entry points. Running forge test with match-contract against the invariant test contract lets you target just that suite.

When an invariant fails, Forge prints the exact call sequence that broke it, so you can reproduce the failure deterministically instead of guessing which of hundreds of random calls caused it. You're ready for Lesson 4 once you can explain why real invariant suites fuzz a handler instead of the target contract directly.
